item.title: Iran says U.S. election results show Americans reject the war
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war: Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that the U.S. midterm election results reflected Americans' rejection of the war President Trump launched against his country. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf added a warning that if Mr. Trump doesn't heed the message from American voters, it would bring "a Nightmare."Mr. Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war was partially to blame for the GOP's resounding midterm election losses. But Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal he didn't regret the conflict and added he "would have done it again."Despite signs of a diplomatic push to reach a peace deal, ships continue to come under attack in the Strait of Hormuz, two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the strait, local media reported Thursday, citing Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corp. And the Guard said Wednesday that four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the waterway.
New Updates
35m ago
Iran says two tankers and tugboat caught fire in Strait of Hormuz
Two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said, local media reported on Thursday.
Since the outbreak of the Iran war on Feb. 28, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
In response, the United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel through the strait. The U.S. Central Command said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the strait since summer.

item.title: French blood banks hit by cyberattack days after European freezer hacks
item.description:
A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.
The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars.
The attacks have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology.
In the most recent cyberattack, the French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said in a statement released late Tuesday "temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels" on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that "no blood products or samples were compromised," it said.
French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 22 Fahrenheit (minus 30 Celsius) to as high as 230 F (110 C).
The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the blood bank said.
Filled blood collection bags from a blood drive organized by the French Blood Establishment are seen in Poitiers, France, Sept. 24, 2026.

item.title: Ukraine says "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70
item.description:
Kyiv — The death toll from a Russian missile strike on a Ukrainian aid distribution center climbed to 40, President Zelenskyy said in a Wednesday post on social media. Zelenskyy said Russia dropped nine bombs on an old school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Ukraine's southeast Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.
"They first struck people who had come to receive humanitarian aid, and then first responders and police officers who arrived at the scene," Zelenskyy wrote, noting that rescue efforts were still ongoing Wednesday afternoon, and "more than 30 people may still be under the rubble."
Russia's Defense Ministry said a strike in the area targeted Ukraine's military, and it claimed that as many as 25 Ukrainian service members were killed. Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians, despite strikes regularly hitting apartment buildings and other civilian infrastructure.
A view of the destruction from Russian airstrikes on Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region Nov. 2, 2026, as the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry said Russian forces repeatedly struck a school where local residents regularly gathered to receive humanitarian aid.
UKRAINIAN STATE EMERGENCY SERVICE/Anadolu/Getty
On Tuesday, Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the year on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting facilities in 10 different regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry.
The attacks affected the Ukrainian capital's water supply, with Kyiv residents losing running water in their homes for more than 16 hours. Kyivvodokanal, the city's water utility, said water supply and sewage pumping stations in Kyiv resumed operations on Wednesday afternoon.

item.title: Hackers can hijack grocery store freezers. What about our homes?
item.description:
London — Cyberattacks on grocery store refrigeration systems across Europe sent temperatures soaring on Monday, spoiling food and causing significant financial losses in the second such incident in less than a month. In October, hundreds of French stores were targeted in a similar attack that sent temperatures in some units soaring to 122° Fahrenheit, destroying a huge amount of food.
On Wednesday, France's health service said the country's national emergency blood supply network had also been compromised by hackers this week, though alert and backup systems prevented cold storage facilities from being shut down, and no supplies were lost.
The incidents have renewed wider concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the growing risks of internet-connected consumer "smart" technology. It is not just essential systems such as electricity grids, healthcare databases and grocery store chains' refrigeration, which can have multiple layers of security and redundancy built in, but everyday appliances that are now connected to the internet.
Employees throw away bags of spoiled food outside an ICA supermarket on in Stockholm on Nov. 2, 2026, after stores suffered problems with their refrigerators and freezers.
Fredrik SANDBERG/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty
The concern among some experts is that devices pitched as time-saving conveniences for consumers could also create potential entry points for hackers.
CBS News spoke with several cybersecurity experts who warned that similar vulnerabilities to those exploited in the grocery store hacks could exist in our homes. From heating systems and smart TVs to security cameras, door locks and ovens, millions of household appliances are now online.

item.title: Mother, daughter dead in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
item.description:
A mother and daughter are dead in a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, British Columbia, devastating their family, according to the victims' relatives and B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
Family members identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed.
The victims were first reported missing on Nov. 1, after they failed to return from what was expected to be a short afternoon walk.
"The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them," said Josh Balcarras, Balcarras' brother, in an interview with CBS News Canadian partner CBC News. "That turns into a day, and then a night … then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing."
Balcarras' body was discovered in the Snooka West Trail area on Monday afternoon. Reed's remains were found on Tuesday. Agencies including the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and local search and rescue authorities took part in the investigation, said Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service. Tyre announced the discovery of the two sets of the remains on social media.
A grizzly bear walks along a fallen tree in British Columbia, Canada.
Matthew Bailey/VWPics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
"Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time. We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident," Tyre said in one video.
Tyre said it is not clear how many bears were involved. Efforts to locate and capture any involved animals are underway, he said. Captured bears will be assessed. item.title: How other countries are reacting to the U.S. election results
item.description:
The Iranian regime was quick to label the resounding losses for President Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections as evidence of American voters rejecting the costly war he launched with Israel more than eight months ago.
Spain's leader called it a sign of a global, right-wing populist "wave" crumbling, and Russia acknowledged that it "could complicate relations with the U.S."
Below is a look at those statements and other reactions from foreign leaders and figures, including some hopeful leaders as elections loom in other countries.
Iran
A statement attributed to Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Wednesday made it clear that Tehran is not expecting the outcome of the U.S. elections to change Washington's approach more than eight months into its war with Iran:
"If there are still people who harbor even the slightest hope for a change in behavior or for party and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who believe that by making concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken," the statement published on Khamenei's official website said.
Earlier, Iran's chief negotiator said the results reflected Americans' rejection of the war with his country.
"Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X. He cited the increased cost of living, or "conscience," as two possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added as a warning.
Russia
In Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hoped President Trump would still be able to "continue his peace-making efforts" in the wake of the U.S. elections.

item.title: Stranded U.S. cruise ship departs Cambodia with no passengers
item.description:
A U.S. cruise ship that forced all its passengers to disembark in Cambodia after suspending its operations last week has departed the Southeast Asian nation with only crew aboard, Cambodian officials said Wednesday.
The MV Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs.
It had been docked for a scheduled stop at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, when on Oct. 28 its 203 passengers were suddenly told they had to disembark within a few hours.
The ship left Sihanoukville late Tuesday with only crew and other personnel on board, said Tang Sochetkresna, director of the Tourism Department of Preah Sihanouk province. He said he didn't know the ship's next destination, but multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News the ship will be moved to Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned off.
The cruise ship is now under control of its lender, according to a message sent to residents and obtained by CBS News. Company leadership, however, said they're optimistic they can get the ship back — if they find an operational partner.
A drone view of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship departing from Sihanoukville Autonomous Port without passengers after residents living aboard the vessel were forced to disembark in Preah Sihanouk province, Cambodia, November 4, 2026.
SOVEIT YARN / REUTERS
"This is a 30- to 90-day process, and, during that process, we have time to get a restructure done," Mike Petterson, the company's founder and executive chairman, told CBS News.
